text: 3608–17. Malignant neoplasms of the breast. Cancer of the breast is the most common malignant neoplasm in women. The disease is rare under the age of 25, and increases in incidence with age, although the rate of increase slows af- ter the menopause. Risk factors include a family history (women with inherited BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutations are at higher risk), and reproductive hormonal factors such as early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, and older age at birth of first child. Oral contraceptives and postmeno- pausal HRT are also associated with a small excess risk (see Carcinogenicity, Breast, on p.2059 and p.2071 respec- tively). Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) is a tumour localised to the breast ducts with no evidence of invasion. Invasive breast cancer can be divided into three main groups: • early breast cancer (operable, primary, stage I/II) • locally advanced disease (inoperable local, stage III) • advanced disease (metastatic; stage IV) Breast cancer is an extremely heterogeneous disorder, and the clinical course is consequently very variable; such fac- tors as patient age and menopausal status, tumour size and grade, involvement of axillary lymph nodes or skin, and presence of hormone receptors within the tumour may be a guide to the extent and aggressiveness of disease, and hence have prognostic significance for treatment.1-3 Early testing for overexpression of HER2 (human epidermal growth factor receptor-2) is increasingly important, since it is of value in determining response to certain treat- ments.3 Up to 20% of all cancers of the breast detected by mam- mographic screening are ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS),4-7 the management of which still has some areas of controversy. Most patients with DCIS will be offered breast-conserving surgery,3,6,8 although mastectomy, which was historically preferred, is still the treatment of choice in high-risk patients.3-7 Radiotherapy is usually rec- ommended after successful breast-conserving surgery,3,6,8 as it reduces the rate of recurrence and the risk of develop- ing invasive disease (although it does not affect survival); there may be a subgroup of women in whom it is unneces- sary, but there is controversy as to how to define the group. In the USA the use of adjuvant tamoxifen is also suggest- ed,3-5 but studies have produced conflicting reports of ben- efit on recurrence,5,7 and again, there is no proven effect on survival; French guidelines suggest that the use of adju- vant hormonal therapy be confined to clinical trials.6 Ad- juvant use of newer oestrogen modulators such as anastro- zole is also under investigation.5,7 In patients with early disease (stage I or II; a relatively small tumour with no or limited nodal involvement) the prognosis is fairly good.
